Front: In a series circuit with two identical lamps, how is the supply voltage shared?

Extra cue: At Year 7 level, remember that series components share voltage.
Choices: It is shared between the lamps.|Each lamp gets twice the supply voltage.|Voltage is used up before the first lamp.|Voltage only exists in wires.

Front: In a parallel circuit, what voltage do identical branches connected across the same cell get?
Back: The same voltage across each branch.
Extra cue: Parallel branches are connected across the same two points of the supply.
Choices: The same voltage across each branch.|Zero voltage in every branch.|Half the voltage only in the top branch.|Voltage becomes current.

Front: Why should you not use electrical equipment with wet hands?
Back: Water can help current pass through you, increasing shock risk.
Extra cue: Keep water away from mains electricity.
Choices: Water can help current pass through you, increasing shock risk.|Water makes wires insulating.|Wet hands reduce voltage to zero.|Wet hands make a circuit parallel.

Front: Why should sockets not be overloaded?
Back: Too much current can overheat wires and cause a fire.
Extra cue: This is why fuses and circuit breakers are used.
Choices: Too much current can overheat wires and cause a fire.|It makes the pH too high.|It makes the circuit diagram abstract.|It makes bulbs become acids.

Front: What should you do before changing components in a school circuit?
Back: Switch off the power supply.
Extra cue: This reduces the risk of short circuits or shocks.
Choices: Switch off the power supply.|Add water to the wires.|Use the highest voltage setting first.|Hold both terminals with wet hands.

Front: Why are cells safer than mains electricity for school circuits and toys?
Back: Cells usually provide a much lower voltage.
Extra cue: Lower voltage reduces the risk of dangerous shocks.
Choices: Cells usually provide a much lower voltage.|Cells are always pH 7.|Cells contain no energy.|Cells make circuits incomplete.

Front: What does a fuse do if the current gets too high?
Back: It melts and breaks the circuit.
Extra cue: A fuse protects against too much current.
Choices: It melts and breaks the circuit.|It makes current larger.|It turns blue litmus red.|It measures voltage.

Front: What does a circuit breaker do if current gets too high?
Back: It cuts off the current.
Extra cue: Circuit breakers can be reset after they trip.
Choices: It cuts off the current.|It makes a salt.|It pumps blood.|It measures pH.

Front: What happens to resistance when wire length increases, if material and thickness stay the same?

Front: What can affect the resistance of a wire?

Front: Why are house lights usually wired in parallel rather than series?
Back: Parallel wiring lets each light have its own branch, so lights can be switched independently and one broken lamp does not turn all the others off.
Extra cue: This matches the revision pack idea that branches stay on when another branch breaks.

Front: How can a variable resistor control a lamp or motor?
Back: Changing resistance changes the current, which can change lamp brightness or motor speed.
Extra cue: Higher resistance usually means lower current.
